newsitem.title: UK: London's Big Bang timetable runs many years.
newsitem.headline: London's Big Bang timetable runs many years.

text.p: It was the reforming 1980s government of British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher that took a torch to the web of regulation in the London financial markets 10 years ago this week.
Thatcher and her Chancellor Nigel Lawson initiated the "Big Bang" financial revolution, sparking an upheaval in London share and bond trading which is far from over.
As Lawson wrote in his autobiography:

"The old system had many virtues but in addition to being intellectually indefensible it had one fatal practical defect: it was woefully undercapitalised...while the City of London remained one of the world leaders -- if not the world leader -- across a whole range of financial markets, such as the foreign exchange market, in the securities market it was in danger of becoming a backwater."
The following is a timetable of the Big Bang reforms and subsequent changes:
* 1979: Office of Fair Trading begins investigation into London Stock Exchange Restrictive practices, shortly before Thatcher government elected.

* 1983: Talks between UK government and London Stock Exchange chairman Nicholas Goodison culminate in agreement for LSE to reform itself. Government sets October 27 1986 deadline for introducing package of reforms.

* 1986: "Big Bang" ends brokers' fixed commissions and ends distinction between brokers and share traders, or jobbers. It also transfers membership of Exchange to firms rather than individuals, allowing UK and foreign banks to enter market by buying UK houses. Also ushers in "Seaq" computer trading system.
* 1987: London Stock Exchange trading floor closes.
* September 1995: Tradepoint share trading system starts, for first time allowing automated share dealing in London.
* November 1995: LSE board votes to go ahead with Sequence 6, part of a replacement to Seaq which will allow automated share trading similar to Tradepoint.
* January 1996: LSE chief executive Michael Lawrence ousted after dispute with some leading firms about strategy.
* January 1996: LSE publishes discussion paper on trading reform and launches consultation exercise to gather views of brokers and fund managers.
* Autumn 1997: Automated or "order-driven" trading due to be introduced in a process seen as "Big Bang 2".
